content.thinking:
I notice the investigator queried metrics anchored on one timestamp while the actual alert fired at a different, later time—a mismatch worth flagging. This suggests the anchor point used for the query may have been wrong relative to the alert, though I should treat this as an assumption rather than a confirmed fact.

The chain shows errors exceeded threshold but impact remains unclear since the diagnosis stalled: the metrics query returned nothing because it was anchored at the wrong time relative to the alert, and flag history was empty before the issue got escalated. Root cause is genuinely undetermined—I should be honest that the investigation lacked evidence rather than speculate further.

I need to describe duration and timing using placeholder references rather than actual figures, and number action items starting fresh since none currently exist—proposing things like anchoring metric queries to alert time with loud failure on empty results, enriching alerts with error rate data, and falling back to logs or deployment signals when metrics are unavailable. I'll tie contributing factors back to these action items and cite only the relevant chain references, leaving out the one that doesn't apply.

action_items.item: Anchor the investigator's metrics query on the alert's raised time. Treat an empty result as a retrieval failure, not as 'no data', and retry with a widened window before forming candidates.
Add fallback evidence sources for the investigator for when metrics are unavailable: recent deploys, application logs and a direct health probe of the service. Record which sources were tried.
Change the escalation hand-off so it states which evidence could not be read and why, and pages a named on-call person to read the metrics by hand.
Put the current error rate and its start time in the alert payload, so impact can be reported even when the metrics store cannot be queried afterwards.

causal_chain.step: Users of io-shop saw errors, and the error-rate alert fired. The service was still failing at the last reading, so it was broken for at least {duration}. The size of the error rate and the number of users affected are unknown.

Argus did not identify a cause or take any mitigating action. The investigation produced only a placeholder statement that no cause was determined, and the incident was escalated as having insufficient evidence.
The investigator had no metrics to work from. It read back {T5.2} minutes of data, so it could not see when errors began, how bad they were, or what changed.

The metrics query was anchored on {T4.2}, which does not match the time the alert was raised ({alert_raised}). That mismatch is the most likely reason the query returned nothing. The record does not show why that anchor was chosen.
No second source of evidence was available either. The flag provider's history showed {T7.2} recent changes, so there was no change to point to or roll back.

contributing_factors.factor: The investigator's metrics query used a time anchor that did not match the alert, and an empty result was accepted without being treated as a failure. Nothing checked the query window against the alert time or retried it.

When metrics were missing, Argus had no fallback evidence source, such as logs, recent deploys or the service's own health endpoint. It escalated after only {held} with nothing to hand to the responders.
The escalation carried no useful context and no one was assigned to read the metrics by hand, so the service may have stayed broken until someone picked it up.

input.executive_summary: An alert reported that io-shop was returning too many errors. Argus took the alert up and asked its investigator to look at the service's metrics. The query came back empty, and the flag provider showed no recent changes, so there was nothing to base a diagnosis on. Argus escalated to people after {held}. The service had not recovered when Argus stopped reading, so it was broken for at least {duration}. That figure is a lower bound. The size of the error rate and the number of users affected are unknown because the metrics could not be read. Argus took no mitigating action, and the underlying fault is still unexplained.

got_lucky: The flag history was empty, so Argus had no change that it could have wrongly blamed and rolled back on no evidence.
went_well: Argus received the alert promptly and escalated rather than guessing at a cause or acting on no evidence.
The candidate stated plainly that no cause was determined, so the record does not claim a cause it does not have.
went_wrong: The metrics query returned {T5.2} minutes, so the investigation had no data and ended without a diagnosis.
Impact could not be measured: the error rate and the number of users affected are unknown.
Escalation came without any useful evidence for the people who took over.

input.root_cause: The cause of the io-shop errors was not determined. The investigation had no evidence: its metrics query was anchored on {T4.2}, which is not the time of the alert, and it returned {T5.2} minutes of data. The flag history was also empty, so Argus escalated instead of diagnosing.
